newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Nationsbank CEO sees more U.S. bank mergers.
newsitem.headline: Nationsbank CEO sees more U.S. bank mergers.

text.p: Hugh McColl, chairman and chief executive of NationsBank Corp., said it was not unreasonable to expect the creation of a U.S. bank with assest of $400-500 billion before year 2000 as consolidation continues in the industry.

McColl also said in the text of a speech to bankers at the International Monetary Conference (IMC) that it was likely that the number of U.S. banks playing a significant role overseas was likely to remain flat or even shrink.
"U.S. banks will not become important internationally until they are more important nationally," McColl said.

He said there were good arguments that only one or two U.S. commercial banks, combined with three to four large investment banking firms, have the kind of credibility that makes them "unquestioned global providers."
"Is the creation of a $400- or $500-billion U.S. bank beyond the realm of reason? Again, probably, not," McColl said.
Currently, the top five U.S. banks all top $220 billion in assets.

He said said there was no need for U.S. banks to become massively larger to compete as size could also become a liability and one of the best arguments against size is the drive to make bank balance sheets work harder and better.
Instead, the three factors that would drive success was capital, customers and credibility.
He noted that capital was critical to strengthen U.S. banks growing role in investment banking and they will need this to survive in the full-scale consolidation of the financial services industry.
He added that the top eight U.S. commercial banks hold capital of $116 billion, compared with $30 bilion by top eight U.S. securities firms, so "the outlook is excellent."

The best use of this capital right now is for commercial banks to build larger customer bases by buying those that other's have built up and in the medium-term U.S. banks will grow as a by-product of the quest to build larger customer bases.

The opportunity for U.S. banks to participate in international transactions is largely defined by the needs of its customers, and "this eliminates a larger percentabge of U.S. commercial banks," he said.
For NationsBAnk, this means that it would build expertise in Latin America as most of the large corporations it serves are located in Florida and Texas.
"Even with these opportunities, the number of U.S. banks playing significant roles overseas is likely to remain flate or even shrink as the industry consolidates," McColl said.
